# Compliance Requirements and Enforcement for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
Companies deploying AI hiring tools face substantial obligations under the EU AI Act because employment-related AI systems are presumptively classified as "high-risk" under Annex III, triggering requirements around risk management, human oversight, and record-keeping (high confidence). However, significant uncertainty surrounds the applicable compliance timeline due to a contested "Digital Omnibus" deferral, and no source confirms any concrete enforcement action—fines or investigations—has yet been taken against a company for a hiring AI tool.

## Key Findings

### Classification as High-Risk
AI hiring and recruitment systems are explicitly listed in Annex III as high-risk categories under the AI Act, subjecting them to additional obligations unless an exemption applies (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3), [artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3)). Article 6(3) provides a narrow derogation allowing a system to escape high-risk classification if it does not pose significant risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights, including where it does not materially influence decision outcomes (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6), [Orrick](https://ai-law-center.orrick.com/eu-ai-act/high-risk-ai)). One lower-confidence source suggests that profiling of natural persons automatically removes this derogation, meaning hiring tools that profile candidates would remain high-risk regardless of their apparent limited role (low confidence) ([Questa AI](https://www.questa-ai.com/privacy-cafe/eu-ai-act-countdown-is-your-annex-iii-system-ready-for-august-2)).

### Provider Obligations
Providers of high-risk AI systems must implement a risk management system, data governance measures, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency/instructions for use, and human oversight mechanisms (Articles 9–14) (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk Recital 57](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/recital-57), [CloseIT](https://www.closeit.co/eu-ai-act/article-6-high-risk-classification), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). Additional obligations reportedly include conformity assessment, CE marking, EU database registration, corrective action, and incident reporting, though this is drawn from a single lower-confidence source (low confidence) ([ModelOp](https://www.modelop.com/ai-governance/ai-regulations-standards/eu-ai-act)).

### Deployer Obligations
Companies deploying (rather than providing) hiring tools must use systems per provider instructions, ensure human oversight by trained, competent personnel with authority to intervene, and maintain logs, independent of whether providers completed their own conformity obligations (low confidence) ([FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf), [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)). Deployers may also face fundamental rights impact assessment obligations (low confidence) ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-provider-deployer-obligations)). One medium-confidence interpretive source recommends that vendors document any Article 6(3) derogation claims and that companies establish meaningful human-in-the-loop oversight, training managers to challenge algorithmic outputs (medium confidence) ([Futurium/EC](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass)).

### Timeline and the Digital Omnibus
The Act entered into force August 1, 2024, with prohibitions effective February 2025 and general-purpose AI obligations effective August 2025 (low confidence) ([Warden AI](https://www.warden-ai.com/resources/eu-ai-act-hiring-recruitment)). The original Annex III compliance deadline was August 2, 2026 (low confidence, multiple sources) ([Warden AI](https://www.warden-ai.com/resources/eu-ai-act-hiring-recruitment), [Salt Security](https://salt.security/eu-ai-act-compliance), [Compyl](https://compyl.com/blog/eu-ai-act-penalties)). However, a "Digital Omnibus" reportedly published in the Official Journal on July 24, 2026 pushed the standalone Annex III deadline to December 2, 2027, and Annex I embedded-product AI to August 2, 2028 (low confidence) ([Compyl](https://compyl.com/blog/eu-ai-act-penalties)).

### Enforcement Mechanisms and Penalties
National market surveillance authorities are expected to conduct most enforcement, exercising powers under EU Regulation 2019/1020, with the European Commission/AI Office overseeing certain matters (low confidence) ([Orrick](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2024/09/The-EU-AI-Act-Oversight-and-Enforcement), [Stephenson Harwood](https://www.stephensonharwood.com/insights/the-eu-ai-act-enforcement-overview)). Maximum fines can reach €35 million or 7% of global turnover (low confidence) ([Salt Security](https://salt.security/eu-ai-act-compliance), [RAIL](https://responsibleailabs.ai/knowledge-hub/articles/eu-ai-act-august-2026-compliance)), with Article 99 requiring proportionality in penalty determination (low confidence) ([Compyl](https://compyl.com/blog/eu-ai-act-penalties)). Notably, **no source documents any actual enforcement action, fine, or investigation** taken against a company for an AI hiring tool.

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources conflict on whether the Digital Omnibus deferral is formally adopted (Warden AI, Compyl) or still pending trilogue negotiation with the original 2026 deadline still binding (RAIL) — likely reflecting differing publication dates that cannot be confirmed. Similarly, some sources treat August 2026 as the operative deadline without acknowledging the deferral (Salt Security), while others state it was superseded (Compyl). Multiple claims relating to timelines, provider/deployer obligations, and penalties carry confidence scores below 0.4, reflecting reliance on single, undated blog sources rather than authoritative EU text.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms concrete enforcement actions against hiring AI deployers. The designation status of national market surveillance authorities and whether any have investigated hiring tools remains unclear. The legal status of the Digital Omnibus deferral is unresolved, as is whether interim transparency obligations (e.g., Article 50) apply during any transition period. Guidance on practical regulatory assessment of Article 6(3) derogations and treatment of hiring AI embedded in broader HR software is absent.

# EU AI Act vs. US Federal AI Policy: Foundation Model Provider Requirements

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, detailed legal obligations on general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers, including documentation, copyright compliance, and systemic-risk mitigation, enforced by an EU AI Office (high confidence). Current US federal policy has moved from binding reporting mandates under the 2023 Biden executive order toward deregulation (low confidence) and, more recently, toward a voluntary, national-security-focused framework whose specific provisions carry varying reliability, from medium confidence for its existence to low confidence for its detailed mechanics (see below).

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act: Binding Obligations for GPAI Providers
Under Article 53(1)(a) and Annex XI, GPAI providers must draw up and maintain technical documentation covering training and testing processes and evaluation results (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53), [Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers)). This documentation must be made available to the AI Office, national competent authorities, and downstream providers integrating the model (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)). Providers must also implement a policy for complying with EU copyright law, including honoring rights reservations (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)), and publish a public summary of training content using a mandatory Commission template (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy Template FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/template-general-purpose-ai-model-providers-summarise-their-training-content)). Open-source GPAI models receive partial exemptions from these documentation duties unless they are classified as posing systemic risk (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)). A single lower-authority source claims standard Article 53 obligations took effect August 2, 2025 (low confidence) ([Jaggaer](https://www.jaggaer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-rules-for-general-purpose-ai)).

### EU AI Act: Systemic-Risk Tier
Providers of GPAI models deemed to pose systemic risk face additional obligations under Article 55, including standardized model evaluation, adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity safeguards for model weights and infrastructure (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 55](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-55)). A single legal memo claims these obligations apply once a model meets systemic-risk compute thresholds under Article 51(1)(a) or upon Commission designation (low confidence) ([Quinn Emanuel](https://www.quinnemanuel.com/media/avvj5y50/eu-ai-act-obligations-on-general-purpose-ai-model-providers.pdf)). The same source defines "provider" broadly to include any entity that develops or commissions a GPAI model and places it on the market (low confidence, single source) ([Quinn Emanuel](https://www.quinnemanuel.com/media/avvj5y50/eu-ai-act-obligations-on-general-purpose-ai-model-providers.pdf)).

### US Federal Approach: Distinct Confidence Levels Across Policy Phases
The 2023 Biden EO 14110 required developers of dual-use foundation models and large-scale computing cluster operators to report certain information to the federal government, paralleling elements of the EU's GPAI regime (low confidence, outdated source) ([Clifford Chance](https://www.cliffordchance.com/insights/resources/blogs/talking-tech/en/articles/2024/04/eu-and-us-ai-regulatory-push-overlaps-across-global-business.html)). That EO relied on presidential executive authority to direct agencies rather than legislating directly, unlike the EU's statutory approach (medium confidence, ~0.40) ([DLA Piper](https://knowledge.dlapiper.com/dlapiperknowledge/globalemploymentlatestdevelopments/2023/comparing-the-US-AI-Executive-Order-and-the-EU-AI-Act.html)). In January 2025, President Trump signed EO 14179, reportedly revoking or reviewing EO 14110 and eliminating key federal AI oversight measures in favor of deregulation (low confidence, single source) ([Mind Foundry](https://www.mindfoundry.ai/blog/ai-regulations-around-the-world)).

In June 2026, EO 14409 established cybersecurity mandates and a voluntary framework for frontier AI model security, corroborated across four sources (medium confidence, ~0.56) ([Lathrop GPM](https://www.lathropgpm.com/insights/new-executive-order-signals-evolving-federal-approach-to-ai), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence_in_the_United_States)). Under this framework, developers may voluntarily share new frontier models with the federal government for early access—up to 30 days—before wider release (medium confidence, ~0.48) ([McDermott](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-executive-order-shifts-us-ai-policy-toward-national-security), [A&O Shearman](https://www.aoshearman.com/en/insights/trump-administration-issues-executive-order-on-ai-and-cybersecurity)). By contrast, the specific "covered frontier model" designation mechanism relies on a single source and carries low confidence (~0.12) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence_in_the_United_States)), as does the claim that the EO directs agencies to strengthen federal cybersecurity and prioritize enforcement against AI-enabled cybercrime (low confidence, ~0.12) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence_in_the_United_States)). Readers should treat the framework's broad existence as more reliable than its granular mechanics.

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether Biden-era reporting mandates remain active: an April 2024 Clifford Chance analysis describes them as in force, while a later source indicates they were rescinded or under review by January 2025 ([Clifford Chance](https://www.cliffordchance.com/insights/resources/blogs/talking-tech/en/articles/2024/04/eu-and-us-ai-regulatory-push-overlaps-across-global-business.html) vs. [Mind Foundry](https://www.mindfoundry.ai/blog/ai-regulations-around-the-world)). More fundamentally, the EU's binding regulatory model contrasts with the US's explicitly voluntary framework—a philosophical rather than factual divergence ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/53) vs. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence_in_the_United_States)). Multiple US-policy claims fall below the 0.4 confidence threshold, including the EU's August 2025 effective date, systemic-risk trigger timing, provider definition, EO 14179 details, the "covered frontier model" designation, and EO 14409's cybercrime-enforcement provisions—these should be treated as unverified pending corroboration.

## Knowledge Gaps
The substantive content of the US "covered frontier model" voluntary framework remains undefined, as does its comparability to EU adversarial testing and incident-reporting requirements. No source confirms binding federal legislation analogous to the AI Act exists in the US, nor do sources address enforcement penalties for the US framework, interactions between the 2025 and 2026 EOs, state-level US AI laws, or quantitative comparison of EU compute thresholds to US frontier-model criteria.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act, and the Status of Notified Body Designations

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act's sectoral conformity assessment route for Annex I Section A products is well-established in authoritative EU guidance (high confidence), whereas the specific routing rules for standalone Annex III systems—which route requires internal control versus notified-body assessment for each category—rest primarily on lower-authority blog sources and remains only weakly supported (low confidence) [AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment). The practical ecosystem of designated notified bodies appears immature and poorly documented in available sources, creating significant uncertainty for providers approaching the August 2026 compliance deadline (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
For high-risk AI systems already covered by sectoral product legislation listed in Annex I Section A, providers must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies also verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai). For Annex III (standalone high-risk) systems, Article 43 is described as providing two routes: internal control under Annex VI (self-assessment) or third-party assessment under Annex VII involving a notified body (low confidence) [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [EU AI Act](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment).

For Annex III point 1 biometric systems specifically, providers may use internal control if harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied; otherwise, notified-body assessment is mandatory (low confidence) [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-requirements-process-guide). For Annex III points 2–8, internal control under Annex VI is generally sufficient, allowing self-assessment (low confidence) [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-requirements-process-guide).

Under Annex VII, the notified body assesses the quality management system and technical documentation and conducts ongoing surveillance (low confidence) [EU AI Act](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment), and separately, notified bodies verify compliance of the quality management system with Article 17 and examine technical documentation against essential requirements in Chapter III (low confidence) [Securiti.ai](https://securiti.ai/eu-ai-act/article-43). Notably, Annex VII para 4.5 permits notified bodies, upon reasoned request and as a last resort, to access training and trained models including parameters, subject to IP and trade secret protections (medium confidence) [Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7).

### Related Legal Provisions
Article 44 governs certificates, Article 45 covers notified body information obligations, Article 46 provides derogation, Article 47 requires an EU declaration of conformity, and Article 48 requires CE marking (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk - Article 60](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-60). Article 46 allows market surveillance authorities to authorise placing a specific high-risk system on the market for a limited period, by derogation, for exceptional reasons of public security, health, or environmental protection (medium confidence) [Article 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46). A new conformity assessment is required after substantial modification, unless changes were predetermined and documented in the initial technical documentation (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43). Technical documentation and QMS records must be retained for ten years (low confidence) [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-requirements-process-guide).

### Notified Body Designation Status
As of early-to-mid 2026, the pool of formally designated notified bodies remains very small, creating practical difficulties for providers requiring third-party assessment (low confidence) [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-what-providers-must-do-zunic-maric-0dfof). Designation processes across member states are described as ongoing, with limited capacity and uncertain timelines despite the fixed August 2026 compliance deadline (low confidence) [eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act). Ireland has taken a decentralised approach, designating 15 existing bodies as market surveillance authorities under Statutory Instrument No. 366 of 2025 (medium confidence) [National Implementation Plans](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/national-implementation-plans); a National AI Office is separately expected to be established by August 2026 as the central coordinating authority (low confidence) [Ireland DETE](https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/what-we-do/innovation-research-development/artificial-intelligence/eu-ai-act).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources describing the November 2022 proposal text of Article 43 differ from those describing the finalized adopted framework; using proposal-era language as current law would be outdated [Proposal Article 43](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html) vs. [EU AI Act](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment). Multiple claims fall below 0.4 confidence, including Annex III category-by-category routing rules (claim_002, 0.34; claim_003, 0.34; claim_004, 0.12), Annex VII procedural details (claim_005, 0.12; claim_010, 0.24), and all notified-body-scarcity and Irish AI Office timeline claims (claim_013, 0.12; claim_014, 0.12; claim_016, 0.12); these rely on non-authoritative blog sources rather than official EU texts and should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source identifies specific notified bodies formally designated under the AI Act, nor provides an official registry count or country breakdown. It remains unclear how many Annex III categories currently have any operational notified bodies. The interaction between Article 46 derogations and capacity shortages is undocumented, as is whether enforcement discretion or grace periods will apply given the shortage ahead of the August 2026 deadline. Designation criteria and procedures in member states beyond Ireland are not covered.

# When Do Annex III High-Risk AI Obligations Apply Under the EU AI Act?

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act as originally adopted set 2 August 2026 as the application date for high-risk AI system obligations under Annex III (medium confidence) ([Implementation Timeline](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation-timeline), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/04/us-companies-face-eu-ai-acts-possible-august-2026-compliance-deadline)). However, a subsequent legislative amendment—the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), which entered into force on 27 July 2026—reportedly postponed this deadline to 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2)/Annex III systems (low confidence) ([ISMS Copilot](https://www.ismscopilot.com/learn/eu-ai-act-what-applies-from-2-august-2026), [Questa AI](https://www.questa-ai.com/privacy-cafe/eu-ai-act-countdown-is-your-annex-iii-system-ready-for-august-2)). Given the timing of this amendment relative to source publication dates, there is significant confusion in available materials, and the current authoritative status of the deadline cannot be confirmed with high confidence from the sources reviewed.

## Key Findings

### Original Statutory Timeline
Under Article 113 of the AI Act as originally adopted, obligations for high-risk AI systems under Annex III were set to apply from 2 August 2026, with a later date of 2 August 2027 reserved for Annex I product-integrated systems under Article 6(1) (medium confidence) ([Implementation Timeline](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation-timeline), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/04/us-companies-face-eu-ai-acts-possible-august-2026-compliance-deadline), [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)). Article 111(2) further clarifies that the Regulation applies to high-risk systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 only if they undergo significant design changes after that date, with distinct rules for systems used by public authorities (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Article 111](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-111)).

### Reported Postponement via Digital Omnibus
Several sources report that Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the "Digital Omnibus on AI"), entering into force 27 July 2026, amended Article 113 to postpone application of Chapter III Sections 1–3 for Annex III high-risk systems to 2 December 2027, and for Annex I systems to 2 August 2028 (low confidence) ([ISMS Copilot](https://www.ismscopilot.com/learn/eu-ai-act-what-applies-from-2-august-2026), [Questa AI](https://www.questa-ai.com/privacy-cafe/eu-ai-act-countdown-is-your-annex-iii-system-ready-for-august-2), [Ovidiu Suciu](https://ovidiusuciu.com/eu-ai-act/eu-ai-act-article-113-entry-into-force-application)). One legal-analysis source suggests this deferral was justified by delays in the availability of harmonized standards, common specifications, guidance, and national competent authority establishment, which jeopardized effective enforcement (low confidence) ([Akin Gump](https://www.akingump.com/en/insights/alerts/EU-AI-act-amendments-defer-and-clarify-obligations)).

### Related Timeline Milestones
Separately, Article 5 prohibitions (items 1–8) took effect in February 2025, with a ninth prohibition introduced via the Omnibus process taking effect in December 2026 (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EU](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), [Ovidiu Suciu](https://ovidiusuciu.com/eu-ai-act/eu-ai-act-article-113-entry-into-force-application)). General-purpose AI (GPAI) obligations became applicable in August 2025 (medium confidence) ([Ovidiu Suciu](https://ovidiusuciu.com/eu-ai-act/eu-ai-act-article-113-entry-into-force-application)). Transparency obligations under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026, with marking/detection requirements under Article 50(2) deferred to 2 December 2026 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk FAQ](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/faq)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
There is a direct and unresolved contradiction in the source set regarding the Annex III application date: numerous sources state 2 August 2026 as operative (medium confidence, e.g., [Belgrave Whitmore](https://www.belgravewhitmore.com/guides/eu-ai-act-high-risk-systems), [Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/artificial-intelligence/ai-governance/eu-ai-act), [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)), while others assert this was postponed to 2 December 2027 by legislative amendment (low confidence, e.g., [ISMS Copilot](https://www.ismscopilot.com/learn/eu-ai-act-what-applies-from-2-august-2026)). This discrepancy appears to reflect a timing issue: sources not accounting for the Digital Omnibus (entered into force 27 July 2026) reflect the outdated pre-amendment date. Claims describing the postponement are flagged as **low confidence** (0.12–0.17) due to limited corroboration from authoritative EU sources, and should be treated with caution pending verification against the official EU AI Act Service Desk or Official Journal text.

## Knowledge Gaps
The full text and precise scope of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 is not available in the reviewed sources, leaving unclear which specific Chapter III provisions are postponed and whether the deferral applies uniformly across all eight Annex III use-case categories. It remains unconfirmed whether interim obligations (e.g., risk management, registration) apply to Annex III systems before 2 December 2027. The interaction between the postponed Annex III deadline and the Article 50 transparency (2 August 2026) and prohibition (2 December 2026) deadlines is not fully reconciled. Further research should consult the official EU Official Journal text of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and updated EU AI Act Service Desk guidance to confirm the current legal status.
